newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels target Kisangani, claim new successes.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels target Kisangani, claim new successes.

text.p: Zairean rebel leader Laurent Kabila said on Sunday he had ordered his troops to halt their advance on the Rwandan Hutu refugee camps at Tingi Tingi.
U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees Sadako Ogata visited Tingi Tingi on Saturday and expressed horror at the condition of the 127,000 refugees trapped there.
She said the fast-moving front line posed a threat to the refugees with the rebels taking Amisi, 70 km (40 miles) down the road to the east.

But Kabila said his forces would not advance further on the refugee camp. They would, he said, be targeting Kisangani, Zaire's third largest city, because government soldiers were killing his supporters there.
"We need to get to Kisangani and liberate the people there. Our people, our supporters are being targeted and killed in Kisangani," he said.
Kabila said he had received reports of looting and killings by the Zairean army in Kisangani as panic gripped the city. He said the reports had forced him to rethink strategy and target Kisangani.

Kabila, speaking to Reuters shortly after midnight at the opulent residence built in Goma for ailing Zairean president Mobutu Sese Seko, said his forces captured the town of Bafwasende, about 250 km (150 miles) east of Kisangani on Friday.

He said forces of his Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL) were now consolidating around the airbase of Kindu, about 340 km (200 miles) west of the Zaire-Rwanda border.
They were also closing in on the Lake Tanganyika port of Moba inside the mineral-rich province of Shaba in Zaire's southeast, he added.
"Our forces have consolidated their positions around Kindu and have moved to within 25 km (15 miles) of Moba," Kabila, surrounded by aides and bodyguards, said.
He said the Zairean army was reinforcing Moba by air. "But these (Zairean) soldiers have no reason to fight so we do not expect any major resistance from the reinforcements," he added.
He said Zaire's mercenary-backed army had used MI-24 Russian helicopter gunships to bomb rebel positions near the town of Lubutu but had failed to dislodge his forces on Friday.
In a humanitarian gesture, he said, he had ordered his troops to halt their advance on refugee camps which he says contain the remains of the Hutu army ousted from Rwanda in 1994.
He said this would give the U.N. refugee agency a chance to sort out the problem of the refugees, many of whom, he says, are militia and former soldiers holding other refugees as hostages.
Kabila's Alliance has eroded Mobutu's control in eastern Zaire since the rebellion began last October. The Alliance claims to control a strip about 1,400 km (875 miles) long.
Mobutu returned home on Friday after medical tests in Europe and a three-day visit to Morocco, a long-time ally.
Kabila said he was prepared to meet Mobutu for talks on how to hand over power but he ruled out Kenya, France and Belgium as possible venues for a meeting.
"These countries have demonstrated open support for Mobutu and cannot therefore be impartial mediators in our conflict," he said.
"We need balanced people, people who will look at Zaire without taking sides," he said, suggesting mediation by South Africa, Zimbabwe, Mozambique and Nigeria.

Several African nations have called for international mediation in a war which was sparked off by Zairean attempts to expel the Banyamulenge -- an ethnic Tutsi group -- back to Rwanda, a land they left up to 200 years ago.
